items.title: 14.3.3 Derivation of Useful Results of Cross Products

blocks.text: By applying the definition of cross product to unit vectors \(\underline{i}\), \(\underline{j}\) and \(\underline{k}\), we have:

blocks.alt: Three axes from the origin O: z upwards, y to the right and x slanting down to the left. Short thick arrows i, j and k of length one lie along the x-, y- and z-axes.
blocks.caption: Figure: unit vectors i, j, k along the axes (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Why: the angle between a vector and itself is \(0^{\circ}\) and \(\sin 0^{\circ} = 0\). A vector is parallel to itself, so (14.3.2) its cross product with itself is the zero vector.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why: \(\underline{i}, \underline{j}, \underline{k}\) are mutually perpendicular, so \(\theta = 90^{\circ}\), \(\sin 90^{\circ} = 1\), and each has length 1. So each product has length 1.
The direction \(\underline{n}\) comes from the right hand rule: fingers along \(\underline{i}\) (the \(x\)-axis), curl towards \(\underline{j}\) (the \(y\)-axis): the thumb points up the \(z\)-axis, so \(\underline{n} = \underline{k}\). In the same way \(\underline{n} = \underline{i}\) for \(\underline{j} \times \underline{k}\) and \(\underline{n} = \underline{j}\) for \(\underline{k} \times \underline{i}\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
The book's line uses \(\sin(-\theta) = -\sin\theta\): turning from \(\underline{v}\) back to \(\underline{u}\) is a turn through \(\theta\) in the opposite sense.
An easier way to see the same result: \(\underline{v} \times \underline{u}\) has the same size \(|\underline{v}||\underline{u}|\sin\theta\), but by the right hand rule (curl from \(\underline{v}\) to \(\underline{u}\)) its direction is \(-\underline{n}\). Hence \(\underline{v} \times \underline{u} = -(\underline{u} \times \underline{v})\).
So the cross product is not commutative; changing the order changes the sign. In particular
\[\underline{j} \times \underline{i} = -\underline{k},\quad \underline{k} \times \underline{j} = -\underline{i}\]
\[\underline{i} \times \underline{k} = -\underline{j}\]

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: The cross product of \(\underline{i}\), \(\underline{j}\) and \(\underline{k}\) are written in the cyclic pattern. The given figure is helpful in remembering this pattern.

blocks.alt: A circle with i at the lower left, j at the lower right and k at the top. Arrows around the circle go from i to j, from j to k and from k back to i.
blocks.caption: Figure: the cyclic pattern i → j → k → i (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
How to read the circle: going round in the direction of the arrows (\(\underline{i} \to \underline{j} \to \underline{k} \to \underline{i}\)) the product of two neighbours is the third one with a plus sign: \(\underline{i} \times \underline{j} = \underline{k}\), \(\underline{j} \times \underline{k} = \underline{i}\), \(\underline{k} \times \underline{i} = \underline{j}\).
Going against the arrows gives a minus sign: \(\underline{j} \times \underline{i} = -\underline{k}\), \(\underline{k} \times \underline{j} = -\underline{i}\), \(\underline{i} \times \underline{k} = -\underline{j}\).

blocks.caption: Row vector × column vector, e.g. row j, column k gives j × k = i (our summary table)

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. \(\underline{i} \times \underline{i} = \underline{j} \times \underline{j} = \underline{k} \times \underline{k} = \underline{0}\).
2. \(\underline{i} \times \underline{j} = \underline{k}\), \(\underline{j} \times \underline{k} = \underline{i}\), \(\underline{k} \times \underline{i} = \underline{j}\) (cyclic order).
3. Reverse order gives a minus sign: \(\underline{u} \times \underline{v} = -\underline{v} \times \underline{u}\).
4. \(\underline{u} \times \underline{u} = \underline{0}\) for every vector \(\underline{u}\).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Writing \(\underline{i} \times \underline{k} = \underline{j}\): the order \(i, k\) is against the cycle, so \(\underline{i} \times \underline{k} = -\underline{j}\).
2. Writing \(\underline{i} \times \underline{i} = 1\) (that is the dot product \(\underline{i} \cdot \underline{i}\)); the cross product gives \(\underline{i} \times \underline{i} = \underline{0}\).
3. Writing \(\underline{u} \times \underline{v} = \underline{v} \times \underline{u}\): the cross product changes sign when the order changes.
